# Alstom Transportation, Inc. v. Federal Railroad Administration, 25-5456 (D.C. Cir. 2026)
**Court:** U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit

**Docket Number:** 25-5456

**Date Decided:** September 25, 2026
A privately owned railroad company was engaged by the Nevada Department of Transportation to build a high-speed passenger rail line between Southern California and Las Vegas, Nevada. To fund this $12 billion project, the company sought and received a $3 billion federal grant from the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.
The railroad company solicited bids for high-speed trains, and only two manufacturers responded: one offering to build most trains domestically but at a lower maximum speed, and another proposing to build the first two trains abroad to meet the project’s higher speed requirement, before shifting production to the U.S. After reviewing the bids, the FRA proposed to waive the Buy America requirement for either bid, but ultimately finalized a waiver only for the foreign-manufactured trains, based on
The railroad company then contracted with the foreign manufacturer. The domestic manufacturer, having lost the contract, challenged the waiver in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, arguing it was unlawful and arbitrary. The district court dismissed the complaint, finding the domestic manufacturer lacked standing.
On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit held that the domestic manufacturer had standing, as it suffered a concrete economic injury traceable to the waiver and redressable by court action. However, the court determined that the waiver was both lawful and reasonable under the statute, as the FRA correctly found no domestic producer could supply the required high-speed trains.
The appellate court affirmed the district court’s judgment, converting it from a jurisdictional dismissal to a decision on the merits.

## DC Circ. Backs Buy America Waiver For Brightline Trains  

By Tom Lotshaw  

Law360 (September 25, 2026, 6:28 PM EDT) - - The D.C. Circuit on Friday rejected Alstom Transportation Inc.'s challenge of a Buy America waiver approved for trains for a high- speed rail project linking Las Vegas to Southern California, holding that the waiver is reasoned and aligns with federal requirements.  

A majority of a three- judge panel agreed with Alstom that a district court judge erred when she ruled the company lacked standing to challenge a waiver that allowed Brightline West to buy foreign- made trains from Siemens Mobility Inc. and still receive a \(\) 3\$ billion federal grant for its rail project, but all the judges held that Alstom's challenge ultimately failed on the merits.

# Todd Overman Examines D.C. Circuit Ruling on Buy America Waivers

Bass, Berry & Sims attorney Todd Overman authored an article for Law360 analyzing the D.C. Circuit’s recent decision upholding a Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) Buy America waiver for Brightline West’s high-speed rail project. He discussed the practical takeaways for domestic manufacturers, recipients of federal funds, and the agencies that administer these requirements.

Todd explained that in Alstom Transportation Inc. v. Federal Railroad Administration, the court ruled that Alstom was entitled to bring its challenge, but it sided with the government on the substance. He noted that the court allowed the FRA to look at what domestic manufacturers are producing today, instead of what a company plans or may be able to build later. He also noted that the decision shows the importance of a well-supported administrative record in the post Loper Bright landscape.

“Domestic manufacturers should develop evidence of existing production capabilities rather than relying principally on plans to develop compliant products,” said Todd.

Todd recommends that agencies and funding recipients tie technical requirements to documented project needs and tailor waivers so they match proven manufacturing constraints. He added that potential challengers need to carefully evaluate standing before contesting a waiver.

The full article, “DC Circ. Ruling Clarifies Standards For Buy America Waivers,” was published on October 26 on Law360 and is available online (subscription required).

Todd also wrote on this topic for the firm’s GovCon & Trade blog: D.C. Circuit Upholds FRA Buy America Waiver for Brightline West High-Speed Rail Project

linkup.title: What Does the D.C. Circuit’s Brightline West Decision Mean for Buy America Waivers? | GovCon & Trade
linkup.snippet:
In *Alstom Transportation Inc. v. Federal Railroad Administration*, the D.C. Circuit concluded that Alstom had standing to challenge the FRA’s Buy America waiver but ultimately sided with the government on the merits.
### How Can Agencies Evaluate Domestic Manufacturing Capabilities?  
One of the key takeaways from the decision is that the FRA could consider **what domestic manufacturers are capable of producing today**, rather than relying on what a manufacturer plans or may be able to produce in the future.  
For domestic manufacturers, that means developing evidence of **existing production capabilities** rather than relying principally on plans to develop Buy America-compliant products.
### What Does the Decision Mean for Buy America Waivers?  
The ruling also offers practical guidance for agencies and recipients of federal funding. Agencies and funding recipients should tie technical requirements to documented project needs and tailor Buy America waivers to reflect demonstrated manufacturing constraints.  
Potential challengers should also carefully evaluate standing and their ability to demonstrate injury before contesting a Buy America waiver.  
The decision is also significant in the post-*Loper Bright* landscape, reinforcing the importance of a well-developed administrative record that supports an agency’s decision-making.  
My full article, **“[DC Circ. Ruling Clarifies Standards For Buy America Waivers](https://www.law360.com/articles/2541274),”** was published October 26 in Law360 and is available online (subscription required).

# ALSTOM TRANSPORTATION INC v. FEDERAL RAILROAD ADMINISTRATION (2026)
## United States Court of Appeals, District of Columbia Circuit.
###
ALSTOM TRANSPORTATION, INC., Appellant v. FEDERAL RAILROAD ADMINISTRATION, et al., Appellees
### No. 25-5456
### Decided: September 25, 2026
### Before: Katsas, Walker, and Garcia, Circuit Judges.

The Federal Railroad Administration awarded Brightline West $3 billion to support construction of a high-speed railroad between Southern California and Las Vegas. The agency waived a statutory requirement that Brightline buy only goods produced in the United States. Brightline then chose to buy trains manufactured abroad by Siemens Mobility, Inc., rather than trains manufactured domestically by Alstom Transportation, Inc. Alstom now challenges the waiver. We hold that Alstom has standing to do so, but its claims fail on the merits.
I
The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act authorizes the Secretary of Transportation to award grants to support intercity passenger railroads. 49 U.S.C. § 24911. The Secretary has delegated responsibility for administering this program to the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA). 49 C.F.R. § 1.89(a).

Alstom Transportation’s lawsuit challenging the decision of the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) to grant a Buy America waiver to Brightline West for its purchase of rolling stock from Siemens Mobility was dismissed on December 16, 2025.
The court concluded that Alstom lacked standing, in principal part because any injuries Alstom suffered were caused not by FRA, but by Brightline’s independent decision to contract with Siemens rather than Alstom.
The case arose from Brightline’s FRA-funded procurement seeking rolling stock for a high-speed rail line between Las Vegas and Southern California. Alstom and Siemens both responded to the procurement and stated that they would need a waiver from Buy America requirements for the trains’ car shells.
On May 1, 2024, after FRA had issued a Notice of Proposed Nonavailability Waiver for either Siemens or Alstom but before FRA published its final waiver, Brightline announced that it had selected Siemens. FRA published a final notice granting a waiver to Siemens on May 24, 2024, and Brightline and Siemens executed a purchase agreement on May 31.
